subject: Cognitive Science
title: Bounded Rationality
description: A micro-lesson that makes Bounded Rationality usable.

hook.text: Classical economics assumed humans weigh all options and pick the best. Herbert Simon said: that's impossible.

buildup.text: We lack the time, information, and brainpower to compute optimal choices. Our rationality is bounded.

discovery.text: Instead, we 'satisfice'—search until we find an option that's good enough, then stop looking.

twist.text: Satisficing often beats optimizing. Maximizers search longer, choose slower, and feel less satisfied.

climax.text: Simon won the Nobel Prize for showing that good-enough decisions usually outperform perfect ones.

punchline.text: Good enough is often better than best.

details.summary: Herbert Simon argued that humans are not perfectly rational but boundedly rational. We lack the time, information, and cognitive capacity to optimize every decision. Instead, we satisfice, choosing options that are good enough.
details.whyItMatters: Bounded rationality explains why humans are not irrational but are working within real constraints. It shifted economics and psychology toward studying how people actually decide.
takeaways: Humans lack the capacity for fully rational optimization
Satisficing means choosing a good-enough option
Simon's insight reshaped economics and decision science

faq.question: What is the difference between optimizing and satisficing?
faq.answer: Optimizing means evaluating every option to find the absolute best. Satisficing means setting a threshold and accepting the first option that meets it. In a complex world with limited time, satisficing is often more efficient and leads to comparable outcomes with less effort.

faq.question: How does bounded rationality differ from irrationality?
faq.answer: Bounded rationality says people are rational within their constraints. Given limited information and processing power, their decisions make sense. Irrationality implies random or senseless choices. Simon showed that heuristics are smart adaptations to cognitive limits, not failures of logic.
